reviews.neutralCapabilitySummary: Select and structure game-agent behavior around readability, deterministic simulation needs, navigation scale, and player-perceived fairness.
neutralIntentExamples: design readable enemy or companion behavior for a game
choose and validate a navigation and decision-making approach for game agents
inputs: agent role and desired player experience
world topology, entity count, timing constraints, and available authoring or runtime data
operations: choose a behavior representation
select a navigation strategy and cache or share its work where appropriate
add telegraphing, reaction windows, coordination limits, and bounded variation
keep model-assisted work outside the real-time state update and validate any state-changing output
outputs: an inspectable agent-behavior design with performance assumptions, fairness checks, and verification questions
failureBehavior: retain uncertainty when player-facing readability or timing has not been playtested
avoid real-time model calls or unvalidated outputs that can mutate simulation state
exclusions: treating apparent intelligence as the primary quality measure
using one navigation algorithm for every topology or population size
invisible difficulty adjustment or instant reactions
usefulInvariants: the simplest adequate behavior model is preferred
agent state is inspectable during debugging
player-readable anticipation and reaction time are part of correctness
runtime state changes are schema-validated and bounded
materialRisks: heuristic timing and thresholds need genre-specific play evidence
shared navigation fields can become stale as obstacles change
variation can undermine determinism or fairness
the source's model boundary does not cover all game-agent architectures

reviews.neutralCapabilitySummary: Provide a broad web-game implementation map spanning browser rendering, simulation primitives, input, audio, multiplayer, optimization, and release concerns.
neutralIntentExamples: outline a browser game implementation using suitable rendering and simulation primitives
identify web-game subsystems and release checks for a small playable project
inputs: game genre, dimensionality, and target browsers or devices
chosen rendering stack, interaction model, asset needs, and distribution constraints
operations: select a browser graphics path
organize input, update, render, physics, audio, and asset concerns
choose a framework or plain API according to scope
check browser/device behavior, performance, and publishing requirements
outputs: a high-level web-game build outline with technology choices, subsystem boundaries, and verification prompts
failureBehavior: defer framework-specific implementation until the actual API and version are verified
flag omitted product requirements instead of treating the generic workflow as a complete design
exclusions: assuming every listed framework or template is interchangeable
treating generic troubleshooting advice as evidence of a fix
using the broad checklist as a substitute for device testing or game-specific design
usefulInvariants: simulation and rendering concerns remain distinguishable
time-based behavior does not depend on frame count
input, browser lifecycle, and audio restrictions are tested on target environments
release decisions follow the chosen platform and scope
materialRisks: the coverage is wide but shallow
framework APIs and browser behavior can drift
multiplayer transport and security require a deeper design
asset and template availability must be checked rather than assumed

reviews.neutralCapabilitySummary: Design a resilient browser game clock with fixed simulation steps, bounded catch-up, interpolated drawing, and mobile lifecycle handling.
neutralIntentExamples: build a stable update and render clock for a browser game
adapt a game loop for backgrounding, touch devices, and high-refresh displays
inputs: render cadence, pause rules, device class, and browser visibility state
operations: accumulate elapsed time
run a capped number of fixed simulation steps
discard excessive backlog safely
interpolate presentation state
reset or pause timing across visibility and focus transitions
bound device pixel ratio and render rate where mobile budgets require it
outputs: a timing design with explicit simulation, rendering, lifecycle, and thermal-budget behavior
failureBehavior: avoid replaying a large background delta
stop or reset simulation when lifecycle state makes elapsed time invalid
treat an unverified lock-and-return scenario as an open test case
exclusions: assuming variable-step integration is safe for all physics
using frame count as game time
forcing a single mobile frame-rate target without product evidence
usefulInvariants: simulation step size is bounded and consistent
catch-up cannot spiral without limit
render interpolation does not alter authoritative simulation
background return and pause behavior are explicit
materialRisks: fixed steps need tuning for the game's simulation cost
dropping backlog changes elapsed simulation and may affect competitive or replay semantics
device heuristics are not a substitute for profiling
browser lifecycle events vary across platforms

reviews.neutralCapabilitySummary: Shape client-side game persistence around versioned schemas, forward migrations, corruption recovery, debounced writes, and recoverable backups.
neutralIntentExamples: design versioned save data for a game that will evolve after launch
plan loading, migration, backup, and corruption recovery for local game progress
inputs: save data model and current schema version
migration history, storage limits, visibility lifecycle, and whether any values have commercial authority
operations: validate the current save shape
apply retained forward migrations
preserve the pre-migration data
recover to a fresh state on malformed input
debounce routine writes and flush on lifecycle events
choose synchronous or indexed storage according to payload size
outputs: a persistence contract with migration coverage, recovery behavior, backup policy, and storage boundaries
failureBehavior: do not partially load invalid data
start from a safe fresh state when parsing or migration fails
keep an explicit unresolved case when an old-version migration lacks a test
exclusions: deleting historical migrations
writing every frame
treating editable client storage as authoritative for paid or competitive values
usefulInvariants: every persisted shape carries a version
migration precedes final current-schema validation
the last known-good input remains recoverable
load failure does not crash the game
materialRisks: migration code becomes permanent compatibility surface
backup semantics can consume quota or retain sensitive data
local storage is synchronous and size-limited
fresh-state recovery can hide data-loss causes without diagnostics

reviews.neutralCapabilitySummary: Investigate game performance with real-device measurements, frame-time distributions, allocation analysis, rendering costs, and adaptive mobile budgets.
neutralIntentExamples: diagnose frame drops and thermal degradation in a browser game
establish measured rendering and entity budgets for a mid-range mobile device
inputs: frame-time samples, memory behavior, draw-call or fill-rate observations, entity counts, and thermal duration
operations: profile on representative hardware
separate allocation, draw, fill, and logic costs
inspect high-percentile frame times and spike patterns
change one performance factor at a time
adapt selected budgets after sustained overrun and remeasure
outputs: a device-grounded performance diagnosis with budgets, prioritized interventions, and repeatable measurements
failureBehavior: reject laptop-only evidence as sufficient for mobile claims
retain the diagnosis as unconfirmed when percentile or thermal data is absent
exclusions: optimizing average FPS while ignoring spikes
assuming automatic degradation is harmless for every game
using fixed particle or DPR limits without target-device validation
usefulInvariants: the test device represents the shipping constraint
hot-loop allocation is measured rather than inferred
render and simulation budgets are explicit
each intervention is followed by a comparable measurement
materialRisks: device populations vary substantially
adaptive quality can alter intended visual or gameplay communication
browser and operating-system work consumes part of the nominal frame budget
single-session measurements may miss long-run thermal throttling

reviews.neutralCapabilitySummary: Choose a multiplayer authority and synchronization model early, then constrain trust, prediction, transport, timing, and failure behavior around it.
neutralIntentExamples: evaluate an appropriate synchronization model for a multiplayer game
define server authority, client prediction, and disconnect behavior for networked play
inputs: simultaneous interaction requirements and competitive or commercial stakes
latency, determinism, state ownership, transport options, and expected disconnect conditions
operations: classify the interaction as asynchronous, lockstep, authoritative client-server, or rollback
assign authoritative fields
design input sequencing, prediction, reconciliation, and remote interpolation
bound messages and validate inputs
test latency, loss, reconnect, and clock behavior
outputs: a multiplayer architecture decision with trust boundaries, synchronization rules, and adversarial test conditions
failureBehavior: stop and resolve the networking model before implementation when real-time interaction is in scope
treat unsupported latency or packet-loss behavior as unverified
exclusions: retro-fitting real-time networking as a small late feature
using client-side anti-cheat as the sole defense
assuming localhost behavior represents mobile networks
usefulInvariants: the authority for damage, inventory, currency, and results is explicit
network cadence is distinct from render cadence
client prediction never overrides authoritative correction
disconnect and clock handling are normal tested states
materialRisks: deterministic lockstep is highly sensitive to platform differences
prediction and rollback increase state-management complexity
transport choice depends on game semantics and deployment constraints
server authority does not eliminate all abuse or denial-of-service concerns

reviews.neutralCapabilitySummary: Unify keyboard, mouse, touch, and controller input behind player intents while accounting for accessibility, browser behavior, device switching, and response feel.
neutralIntentExamples: design a cross-device control layer for a browser game
audit touch, gamepad, keyboard, and mouse behavior for accessibility and responsiveness
inputs: device capabilities, layout constraints, rebinding needs, browser defaults, and response-time goals
operations: map devices into intent state
poll controller state at a stable point
handle touch cancellation and browser gesture suppression
apply analog deadzones and preserve analog magnitude
support rebinding and physical-key semantics
switch prompts without reflowing controls
outputs: an input architecture and platform checklist with measurable usability and latency checks
failureBehavior: keep device-specific behavior out of gameplay systems
flag accessibility or device coverage gaps instead of declaring parity
treat response targets as unverified until measured on target hardware
exclusions: maintaining separate gameplay implementations per device
assuming browser touch defaults are harmless
hardcoding one keyboard layout or controller prompt set
turning analog controls into binary input without intent
usefulInvariants: gameplay consumes intents rather than device APIs
pointer cancellation cannot leave actions stuck
analog direction and magnitude remain meaningful
device changes update affordances without moving the control layout
materialRisks: screen-size and safe-area rules vary by device
rebindable controls require a complete action vocabulary and persistence policy
latency depends on the full render and simulation pipeline
browser support differences need direct testing
